Name: confidence_gated_adaptive_compute
Title: Internal Confidence as a Stop Signal: Mechanistic Adaptive Compute for Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models carry an internal, decodable confidence estimate whose trajectory predicts when additional reasoning stops changing the answer. Reading this internal signal (not output-token entropy) enables adaptive per-problem compute allocation that beats fixed budgets and output-based confidence.
Related Work: Kadavath et al. (2022) P(True) self-eval; Manakul et al. (2023) uncertainty; Zhang et al. (2024) LLM early-exit via output confidence. We use internal activation-based confidence at intermediate reasoning positions and tie its dynamics to answer stabilization, giving a mechanistic stopping rule rather than an output-probability heuristic.
Abstract: Efficient reasoning requires spending compute in proportion to problem difficulty, yet models apply near-uniform effort. We hypothesize that an internal confidence signal-linearly decodable from mid-network activations-rises as the model converges and that its saturation predicts answer stability better than output entropy. We train probes to predict eventual correctness and answer-stability from activations at each reasoning step, then use the probe trajectory as a stopping criterion: halt when predicted confidence plateaus above a threshold. We compare adaptive stopping against fixed token budgets, self-consistency voting, and output-entropy early-exit on accuracy-versus-compute curves. We further analyze the internal confidence signal mechanistically: which components write it, and whether it is the same signal the model uses to decide to backtrack or verify. We test calibration across difficulties, verifying that hard problems receive more steps automatically. If successful, the method allocates compute mechanistically and reveals that models represent a running estimate of solution reliability, unifying interpretability of self-evaluation with practical efficient inference.
Experiments: 1. Generate stepwise traces; at each step, extract activations and force an answer to label step-wise correctness/stability. 2. Train linear/MLP probes to predict correctness and stability from activations per layer/step. 3. Define stopping rule on probe-confidence plateau; sweep thresholds. 4. Compare vs fixed budgets, output max-prob, predictive entropy, self-consistency (5,10 samples) on accuracy vs mean tokens/FLOPs. 5. Calibration: reliability diagrams; correlate steps-used with ground-truth difficulty. 6. Mechanism: locate components writing the confidence direction via attribution; test overlap with commit/verification circuits.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Probes may overfit and fail out-of-distribution; forcing answers per step perturbs generation. Confidence may be poorly calibrated on hard/adversarial items, risking premature stops. Gains over strong self-consistency baselines may be modest. Internal confidence might just track answer stability, weakening the 'reliability estimate' interpretation.
